# Responsible Fleet Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts I through III built the machine learning fleet, coordinated its training, and optimized its deployment. Part IV develops the mechanisms for enforcing the security, privacy, robustness, environmental, and social constraints that have shaped those design decisions from the outset. Their detailed treatment follows deployment because enforcement depends on the infrastructure, training, and operational controls already introduced. Security, privacy, robustness, and sustainability are engineering constraints with the same physical and mathematical force as bandwidth, power, or latency.

The sociotechnical feedback loop is among the hardest engineering problems the fleet poses. Bias cannot be fixed, and a model cannot be secured, with a single algorithm. Responsible operation requires the monitoring, verification, and governance systems that surround the fleet. A system that ignores these constraints fails operationally, through regulatory shutdown, security breach, or environmental exhaustion. The principles below preview the limits that the following chapters make operational. They identify decisions that belong in the initial system requirements even though the mechanisms for evaluating and enforcing them require the full fleet context.

The first boundary is what the fleet can trust. A model's behavior is shaped by far more parties than the team that trains it.

::: {#pri-provenance-bounds-trust .callout-principle title="The provenance bound on trust"}

**Invariant**: A trained model's behavior is a function of every contributor to its data, code, and weights, including training records and labels, preprocessing and training code, software dependencies, pretrained checkpoints, and the hardware and firmware that executed the run. A contributor that cannot be identified and verified can change that behavior without producing a visible failure, so the provenance record bounds how far the model can be trusted.

**Implication**: Poisoning and supply-chain attacks need not crash anything. A small set of crafted training examples or a backdoored checkpoint can shift a targeted decision while aggregate validation accuracy stays unchanged, so clean evaluation results cannot certify integrity. Trust must be established upstream, through signed artifacts, immutable lineage for data and code, controlled dependencies, and verification before an artifact enters training or deployment, and it extends only as far as that record reaches.

:::

The second boundary is what the fleet can reveal.

::: {#pri-information-leakage .callout-principle title="The information leakage invariant"}

**Invariant**: A privacy claim must name the protected unit and the observations available to an adversary. Let $R$ be one protected individual's training record and $O$ an observable model output. Leakage about that record is present when
$$ I(R; O) > 0, $$
but a model's usefulness alone does not imply this condition. Here, $I(\cdot;\cdot)$ denotes mutual information.

**Implication**: Privacy is a budget, not a switch. Post hoc anonymization of input records does not remove sensitive information already memorized in model weights. Systems requiring formal record-level privacy guarantees should use mechanisms such as differential privacy (DP) where appropriate: DP bounds the influence of adding or removing one protected record for a data analysis or training procedure, and interactive query systems must account for composition and may stop answering once the system exhausts the allocated privacy budget.

:::

Privacy defines what the fleet may reveal; robustness defines how reliably it behaves when distributions drift, environments change, or inputs actively probe its weaknesses.

::: {#pri-robustness-compute-penalty .callout-principle title="The robustness compute penalty"}

**Invariant**: Adversarial training buys intrinsic robustness with training compute. It trains on adversarial examples, inputs perturbed within a stated budget so that the model's prediction changes. Projected gradient descent (PGD)-style training finds each perturbation with $\AttackStepsPgd$ inner attack steps, so a batch costs roughly $\AttackStepsPgd+1$ forward-backward passes instead of one. The resulting clean-accuracy and robustness effects depend on the attack strength and training procedure.

**Implication**: Robustness measures consume training or serving resources and must be evaluated against a stated threat model. External guardrails such as input filtering and output verification can complement adversarial training, but their detection errors and latency costs remain part of the system. They do not establish the same guarantee as robustness of the underlying model.

:::

Efficiency gains can also change demand, so lower energy per request does not by itself establish lower fleet energy consumption.

::: {#pri-jevons-paradox .callout-principle title="The Jevons paradox of AI (efficiency trap)"}

**Invariant**: Efficiency improvements can lower unit cost and stimulate demand. In this comparison, total resource consumption rises only when usage grows by a larger factor than resource efficiency improves. The following schematic depicts that rebound scenario, not an inevitable consequence of efficiency:
$$ \text{Efficiency} \uparrow \implies \text{Cost} \downarrow \implies \text{Demand} \uparrow\uparrow $$

**Implication**: Making models 10$\times$ more efficient can increase total usage enough to erase or even exceed the expected energy savings. Sustainability strategies must focus on absolute limits (carbon budgets, renewable sourcing) rather than rate efficiency (FLOP/s per watt) alone.

:::

Responsible operation also requires making social objectives explicit. Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Score balance compares average scores across groups separately among positive and negative outcomes; equalized odds instead compares thresholded error rates. These criteria can conflict, so a fairness requirement must specify which guarantee the system should enforce.

::: {#pri-fairness-impossibility .callout-principle title="The fairness impossibility law"}

**Invariant**: For imperfect risk scores across groups with different base rates, groupwise calibration and equal mean scores across groups within each outcome class cannot all hold simultaneously.
$$ \Pr(Y=1 \mid A=a) \neq \Pr(Y=1 \mid A=b) \implies \text{Trade-off Required} $$
Here, $Y$ is the outcome and $A \in \{a,b\}$ is the group attribute; the implication assumes imperfect prediction and refers specifically to the three score criteria above. Equalized odds at one chosen decision threshold is a different condition.

**Implication**: Under the theorem's conditions, fairness requires an explicit trade-off; there is no criterion-free optimum that selects among incompatible metrics. Engineers must treat fairness metrics like latency budgets: explicit trade-offs chosen by stakeholders, enforced by the system, and monitored for violation. @Sec-responsible-ai provides the full treatment of when the impossibility result applies, including the equal-base-rate and perfect-prediction exceptions.

:::

Those trade-offs cannot be evaluated once and frozen, because deployed systems alter the data and incentives they later observe.

::: {#pri-sociotechnical-feedback .callout-principle title="The sociotechnical feedback invariant"}

**Invariant**: When a deployed model's decisions affect its environment, the probability distribution of future data $p_{t+1}(X)$ depends on the model's past decisions $f_t(X)$.
$$ p_{t+1}(X) = g(p_t(X), f_t(X)) $$
Here, $g$ is the environment's response function, which maps the current data distribution and the model's decisions into the next data distribution. Settings with this feedback, where predictions change the outcomes they predict, are called performative.

**Implication**: Systems whose decisions affect their environments require closed-loop governance. A model that maximizes accuracy on static test data can still degrade the future data distribution it operates on, amplify incentives that bias the next round of data, or destabilize the environment being monitored. Reliability in these settings requires modeling the *feedback loop*, not the *feed-forward inference* alone.

:::

Part IV follows the same constraint-driven logic as the rest of the book. Security and privacy harden the fleet against attack and protect training data from leakage. Robustness asks whether model performance remains stable when inputs, environments, or adversaries change. Sustainability treats planetary-scale infrastructure as an energy and carbon system, not only a performance system. Responsible AI then connects those technical controls to institutional governance. None of these controls is free in C$^3$ terms. Security and robustness spend compute and serving latency on verification, sustainability prices every powered second of the Fleet Law's computation, communication, and synchronization terms, and governance is the coordination that decides when the fleet may run at all. Together, these chapters complete the engineering discipline that turns a capable fleet into a trustworthy one.
